facts.statement: The genus Compsognathus was originally described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1875.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Cope, 1875

facts.statement: The genus Compsognathus was first described by Johann A. Wagner in 1859.
facts.quote: authority: Wagner, 1859

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Compsognathus is Compsognathus longipes.
facts.quote: type_species: Compsognathus longipes

facts.statement: Compsognathus corallestris was named by Bidar and colleagues in 1972 as a synonym of Compsognathus longipes.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Compsognathus corallestrisBidar et al., 1972

facts.statement: Members of the species Compsognathus longipes could grow to approximately the size of a chicken.
facts.quote: Members of its single species Compsognathus longipes could grow to around the size of a chicken.

facts.statement: Paleontologists have found two well-preserved fossils of Compsognathus, one in Germany in the 1850s and another in France over a century later.
facts.quote: Paleontologists have found two well-preserved fossils, one in Germany in the 1850s and the second in France more than a century later.

facts.statement: The German specimen of Compsognathus, number BSP AS I 563, comes from limestone deposits in Bavaria and was part of the collection of Joseph Oberndorfer.
facts.quote: The German specimen (specimen number BSP AS I 563) stems from limestone deposits in Bavaria and was part of the collection of physician and fossil collector Joseph Oberndorfer.

facts.statement: Johann A. Wagner coined the name Compsognathus longipes in 1859 after receiving the specimen from Joseph Oberndorfer.
facts.quote: Oberndorfer lent the specimen to paleontologist Johann A. Wagner, who published a brief discussion in 1859, where he coined the name Compsognathus longipes.

facts.statement: Johann A. Wagner described Compsognathus as a lizard rather than a dinosaur.
facts.quote: Wagner did not recognise Compsognathus as a dinosaur, but instead described it as one of the "most curious forms among the lizards".

facts.statement: Johann A. Wagner published a more detailed description of Compsognathus in 1861.
facts.quote: He published a more detailed description in 1861.

facts.statement: The deposits containing the German Compsognathus specimen date to the latest Kimmeridgian or earlier Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: All possible localities are part of lagoonal deposits of the Painten Formation, and date to the latest part of the late Kimmeridgian or the earlier part of the early Tithonian.

facts.statement: During the Jurassic, the region where the German Compsognathus specimen was found was part of the Solnhofen archipelago.
facts.quote: In the Jurassic, the region was part of the Solnhofen archipelago.

facts.statement: J.G. Baur removed the right ankle of the German Compsognathus specimen for study, and the part was subsequently lost.
facts.quote: The German paleontologist J.G. Baur, who worked as an assistant of Marsh, removed the right ankle from the slab for illustration and study; this removed part got lost since.

facts.statement: John Ostrom thoroughly described both the German and French specimens of Compsognathus in 1978.
facts.quote: John Ostrom thoroughly described the German specimen as well as the newly discovered French specimen in 1978, making Compsognathus one of the best-known small theropods at that time.

facts.statement: John Ostrom concluded that the German specimen of Compsognathus likely belonged to an immature individual.
facts.quote: He also concluded that the German specimen likely belongs to an immature individual.

facts.statement: The larger French specimen of Compsognathus was discovered around 1971 in Canjuers near Nice.
facts.quote: The larger French specimen (Y85R M4M) was discovered in around 1971 in the Portlandian lithographic limestone of Canjuers near Nice.

facts.statement: The French specimen of Compsognathus dates to the lower Tithonian based on ammonite index fossils.
facts.quote: It dates to the lower Tithonian, as indicated by index fossils of ammonites.

facts.statement: The collection containing the French Compsognathus specimen was sold to the National Museum of Natural History in Paris in 1983.
facts.quote: The collection, including the Compsognathus specimen, was sold to the National Museum of Natural History in Paris in 1983.

facts.statement: Alain Bidar and Gérard Thomel described the French specimen as a separate species, Compsognathus corallestris, in 1972.
facts.quote: Alain Bidar and Gérard Thomel, in a brief 1972 description, announced the new find under a separate species, Compsognathus corallestris.

facts.statement: Ostrom, Jean-Guy Michard, and others later reclassified the French specimen as Compsognathus longipes.
facts.quote: Ostrom, Jean-Guy Michard and others have since relabeled it as another example of Compsognathus longipes.

facts.statement: George Callison and Helen Quimby identified the German specimen as a juvenile of Compsognathus longipes in 1984.
facts.quote: In 1984, George Callison and Helen Quimby identified the smaller German specimen as a juvenile of the same species.

facts.statement: The German specimen of Compsognathus is now believed to be a juvenile, which explains why it is often described as chicken-sized.
facts.quote: Many presentations still describe Compsognathus as "chicken-sized" dinosaurs because of the size of the German specimen, which is now believed to be a juvenile.

facts.statement: Jens Zinke assigned forty-nine teeth from the Guimarota coal mine to Compsognathus sp. in 1998, noting they differ from C. longipes teeth due to serrations on the front edge.
facts.quote: Jens Zinke, in 1998, assigned forty-nine isolated teeth from the Guimarota coal mine of Portugal to the genus. Zinke found that these teeth are not identical to those of Compsognathus longipes, having serrations on the front edge, and thus labeled the teeth as Compsognathus sp. (of unknown species).

facts.statement: Until the 1990s, Compsognathus was considered the smallest-known non-avialan dinosaur and was incorrectly labeled as the closest relative of Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: Until the 1990s, it was the smallest-known non-avialan dinosaur, with the preceding centuries incorrectly labelling it as the closest relative of Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: The German Compsognathus specimen was estimated to be 70–75 cm tall and 89 cm long, while the French specimen was estimated to be 1.25 m tall and 1.4 m long.
facts.quote: The German specimen was estimated to be 70–75 cm and 89 cm in length by separate authors, while the larger French specimen was estimated at 1.25 m and 1.4 m in length.

facts.statement: The German Compsognathus specimen was estimated to weigh between 0.32 kg and 0.58 kg, while the French specimen was estimated to weigh between 2.5 kg and 3.5 kg.
facts.quote: The German specimen was estimated to have weighed 0.32 kg and 0.58 kg, and the French specimen 2.5 kg and 3.5 kg.

facts.statement: Compsognathus had small, pointed teeth suited for eating small vertebrates and possibly insects.
facts.quote: The teeth were small and pointed, suited for its diet of small vertebrates and possibly other small animals, such as insects.

facts.statement: The number of digits on the hand of Compsognathus is a subject of scientific debate.
facts.quote: The number of digits on the hand of Compsognathus has been a source of debate.

facts.statement: Karin Peyer reported in 2006 that skin impressions were preserved on the side of the Compsognathus tail starting at the 13th vertebra.
facts.quote: Karin Peyer, in 2006, reported skin impressions preserved on the side of the tail starting at the 13th tail vertebra.

facts.statement: A 2022 review interprets the tail skin impressions of Compsognathus as aberrant bony growths rather than scales because they are texturally and mineralogically indistinguishable from the vertebrae.
facts.quote: A 2022 review of non-feather integument of non-avialan theropods interprets these structures as aberrant bony growths rather than scales, as the structures are "texturally and mineralogically indistinguishable" from the rest of the fossilized vertebrae.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene erected the infraorder Coelurosauria in 1914, which includes Compsognathidae, and this classification has remained in use since.
facts.quote: Friedrich von Huene, in 1914, erected the new infraorder Coelurosauria, which includes the Compsognathidae amongst other families of small theropods; this classification remained in use since.

facts.statement: A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and colleagues examined nine Compsognathus foot bones for stress fractures but found none.
facts.quote: In a 2001 study conducted by Bruce Rothschild and other paleontologists, nine foot bones referred to Compsognathus were examined for signs of stress fracture, but none were found.

facts.statement: Bidar and colleagues argued in 1972 that the French Compsognathus specimen had webbed hands that would have looked like flippers in life.
facts.quote: Bidar and colleagues, in their 1972 description of the French specimen, argued that this specimen had webbed hands which would look like flippers in life.

facts.statement: Ostrom debunked the hypothesis of webbed hands in Compsognathus, noting the forelimb was poorly preserved and the wrinkles were likely sedimentary structures unrelated to the fossil.
facts.quote: Ostrom debunked this hypothesis, noting that the forelimb of the French specimen is poorly preserved, and that the wrinkles extend well beyond the skeleton and thus are likely sedimentary structures unrelated to the fossil.

facts.statement: Compsognathus preyed on small vertebrates, as evidenced by lizard remains found in the stomach of the German specimen.
facts.quote: The remains of a lizard in the German specimen's thoracic cavity show that Compsognathus preyed on small vertebrates.

facts.statement: The French specimen of Compsognathus contained unidentified lizards or sphenodontids in its stomach.
facts.quote: The French specimen's gastric contents consist of unidentified lizards or sphenodontids.

facts.statement: Conrad designated the lizard found in the German Compsognathus specimen as the holotype of a new species named Schoenesmahl dyspepsia.
facts.quote: Conrad made the lizard found in the thoracic cavity of the German specimen of Compsognathus the holotype of a new species Schoenesmahl dyspepsia.

facts.statement: Peter Griffiths interpreted circular irregularities on the German Compsognathus plate as immature eggs in 1993, but later researchers doubted this because the structures were found outside the body cavity.
facts.quote: Peter Griffiths interpreted them as immature eggs in 1993. However, later researchers have doubted their connection to the genus because they were found outside the body cavity of the animal.

facts.statement: Karl Werner Barthel proposed in 1964 that the circular irregularities on the German Compsognathus plate were gas bubbles formed during carcass putrefaction.
facts.quote: In 1964 German geologist Karl Werner Barthel had explained the discs as gas bubbles formed in the sediment because of the putrefaction of the carcass.

facts.statement: The German and French specimens of Compsognathus were found in lagoons between beaches and coral reefs on Jurassic European islands in the Tethys Sea.
facts.quote: Both the German and French areas where Compsognathus specimens have been preserved were lagoons situated between the beaches and coral reefs of the Jurassic European islands in the Tethys Sea.

facts.statement: No other dinosaur fossils have been found with Compsognathus, suggesting it may have been the top land predator on its islands.
facts.quote: No other dinosaur has been found in association with Compsognathus, indicating that these little dinosaurs might in fact have been the top land predator in these islands.

facts.statement: Reisdorf and Wuttke speculated in 2012 about the death and burial events of the German Compsognathus specimen.
facts.quote: Reisdorf and Wuttke, in 2012, speculated about the events that lead to the death and transportation of the specimen to its place of burial.

facts.statement: Physician Moodie suggested in 1918 that the death pose of Compsognathus resulted from opisthotonus, or death throes causing muscle stiffening.
facts.quote: The physician Moodie, in 1918, suggested that the death pose in Compsognathus and similar fossils was the result of an opisthotonus—death throes causing spastic stiffening of the back musculature—while the animal was dying.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Friedrich von Huene challenged the opisthotonus hypothesis, arguing instead that the death pose resulted from desiccation after death.
facts.quote: This hypothesis was soon challenged by paleontologist Friedrich von Huene, who argued that the death pose was the result of desiccation and therefore occurred only after the death.

facts.statement: Peter Wellnhofer argued in 1991 that the death pose of Compsognathus resulted from the elastic pull of ligaments released after death.
facts.quote: Peter Wellnhofer, in 1991, argued that death poses resulted from the elastic pull of the ligaments, which are released after death.

facts.statement: Veterinarian Cynthia Faux and paleontologist Kevin Padian supported the opisthotonus hypothesis in a 2007 study.
facts.quote: The veterinarian Cynthia Faux and the paleontologist Kevin Padian, in a 2007 study that gained much attention, supported the original opisthotonus hypothesis of Moodie.

facts.statement: Ostrom interpreted certain slab structures in 1978 as traces of weathering before fossil collection.
facts.quote: Ostrom, in 1978, interpreted these structures as traces of weathering that took place just before the fossil was collected.

facts.statement: Nopcsa suggested in 1903 that certain slab structures resulted from decomposing carcass tissue.
facts.quote: Nopcsa, in 1903, instead suggested that these structures resulted from decomposing tissue of the carcass.

facts.statement: Reisdorf and Wuttke suggested in 2012 that certain slab structures were remains of adipocere formed before burial.
facts.quote: Reisdorf and Wuttke, in their 2012 study, suggested that the structures are the remains of adipocere (corpse wax formed by bacteria) that formed around the carcass before burial.

facts.statement: Compsognathus was long considered unique for its small size, often compared to that of a chicken.
facts.quote: For a long time, it was considered unique in its small size, which is commonly compared to that of a chicken.

facts.statement: L. B. Halstead described Compsognathus as an amphibious dinosaur capable of feeding on aquatic prey and swimming away from large predators.

facts.statement: Evidence from related species suggests Compsognathus may have been covered in feather-like structures.
